items.title: ‘We’ve Got Time’: Trump Suggests Iran War Will Continue Into 2027
items.standfirst: The President told news outlets that he was not rushing to make any major decisions about renewed fighting until January.
items.content: U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Nov. 16, 2026. —Win McNamee—Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump suggested he is putting off any major decisions on Iran until 2027, amid reports that he’s considering renewed major operations in the war that continues despite repeated promises that it’ll end soon.Speaking to Reuters on whether new major strikes are possible—the U.S. has engaged in limited strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz—Trump, who was en route to Washington following his trip to China, said, “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.” He added: “We’ve got time.”Trump made similar comments in other interviews. “We’ll see what happens after January 1st," the U.S. President told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, just before his summit with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He also told Axios in a phone call Thursday that he was “not rushing into any decision” on Iran.The President initially promised that the war with Iran would only take weeks, but it has dragged on to nearly nine months, though major hostilities have subsided. Trump has previously said that the war would end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, but the impasse between Iran and the U.S. remained. And in the past weeks, he’s alternated between publicly threatening Tehran and holding off on authorizing new strikes at the request of American allies in the Gulf. Israel has reportedly tried to convince Trump of a new joint strike. The New York Times reported that the U.S. President is considering a new round of extensive military strikes on Iran, after Tel Aviv warned of Tehran’s “success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs.” Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister whose premiership is in limbo, is reportedly pushing for a four- to seven-day airstrike campaign on Iran.Axios reported, citing unnamed sources, that the White House sought input from the Pentagon and intelligence experts on how Iran would respond to the strike scenarios prepared by the U.S. military. Axios also reported that any U.S. campaign would involve Israel and could include strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain, energy and other infrastructure, and Iranian military and civilian leaders. The U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress as the American public largely rebuked Trump and the Republican Party following their handling of the Iran war and the economic fallout it caused, could complicate decisionmaking. Before the Nov. 3 elections, Trump said that Iran was willing to strike a deal, but after the GOP’s stunning losses, which Iranian leaders celebrated, the Administration’s messaging pivoted to maintaining economic sanctions and the blockade on Iran.Vice President J.D. Vance has blamed the war for the GOP’s election losses, but still appeared to defend the President’s foreign policy on Iran. The Vice President earlier said there was no difference between the President and members of his Administration on the war, but as Vance voiced his misgivings, Trump ordered the Vice President to shift his focus away from Iran diplomatic negotiations and toward domestic policies.Trump has a small window to push through further military action against Iran before the newly elected Democrats take office in January. On Thursday, the GOP-led U.S. Senate rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war.Trump addresses reported ‘dirty bomb’ threat In the interview with Fox News, Trump said he thinks people should not be alarmed by reports of a planned “dirty bomb” attack on Washington, D.C. A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives like dynamite with radioactive material. “If it does happen, we wipe them out,” Trump said.Trump acknowledged, however, that intelligence indicated Tehran is potentially interested in biological weapons. “Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear,” he said, referring to the damage that the U.S. has claimed it dealt to Iran’s nuclear facilities.Iran’s foreign ministry refuted Trump’s recent statements. “The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar,” spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X. “Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."Baqaei then referred to how the U.S. justified its invasion of Iraq in 2003, alleging that the government of the late Saddam Hussein was developing weapons of mass destruction, which subsequent investigations found to be untrue. “We find ourselves facing ominous new allegations,” Baqaei said, “and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script.”

items.title: Trump Praises Jeffries and Schumer, Sees Room For Deals With Democrats in 2027
items.standfirst: The President said a Democratic Congress may be easier to work with than a Republican one
items.content: President Donald Trump on Friday offered unusually warm praise for the top two Democrats in Congress and suggested that the incoming Democratic majority may prove easier to negotiate with than Republicans.Speaking to reporters in the briefing room, Trump described Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black Speaker of the House, as “streetwise” and “smart,” and also praised the current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, a striking change in tone toward two lawmakers with whom he has repeatedly clashed. Trump also said prominent Democrats had already reached out to him privately about making potential deals next year on health care and immigration.The comments offered one of the clearest indications yet of how Trump intends to navigate a dramatically altered political landscape following the midterm elections, which delivered Democrats control of both chambers of Congress and left the President facing the prospect of two years of legislative gridlock, aggressive congressional investigations, and potentially another effort to impeach him.Trump appeared eager to present himself as a potential negotiating partner, even as he emphasized that he would use his veto power to block legislation he opposed. He suggested that Democratic leaders might eventually conclude that reaching compromises with him would be more productive than repeatedly passing bills he would reject.“If they want to get things done, I want to get things done too,” Trump said. “There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on health care.”Trump declined to identify the Democrats who had contacted him, saying only that they were influential figures interested in discussing two of the most contentious domestic policy questions. “I've been called by a lot of Democrats,” he said. “People that matter, people that have a lot to do, and they want to talk to me about two things in particular: healthcare, because we can do something with healthcare together. Maybe easier than the Republicans trying to ram it through in reconciliation.”It was not immediately clear whom Trump had spoken with or whether substantive negotiations had begun. Jeffries said earlier this month that he had not spoken with the President since the election.Still, Trump’s remarks came as Democrats have begun assembling a legislative agenda that will test whether their sweeping electoral victory can translate into tangible policy achievements with a Republican president in the White House.Health care, in particular, has emerged as a potential area of overlap, though significant disagreements remain over how far the federal government should go in expanding coverage and how to pay for it.Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is expected to chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take power in January, has proposed a four-year transition toward Medicare for All. His plan would begin by lowering the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expanding benefits to include dental, vision and hearing care, and guaranteeing health coverage for children through age 18.Jeffries has also indicated a willingness to pursue some of those priorities. This week, he said Democrats were preparing proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age, expand benefits and ensure health coverage for children. He has pledged to move quickly to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts enacted under Republican control.Sanders has said that Trump might be more receptive than many Republicans assume. "Trump may be crazy, but he's not stupid, and he is a good politician,” Sanders said in a podcast posted to his YouTube page. “If we were to pass something that guaranteed healthcare to all people, that was enormously popular, and Trump says, 'I'm vetoing it.' Not a smart political move.”Sanders added: "He may say, 'Well, I don't like this or that, let's sit down and negotiate it, but maybe I will sign something.' I think that's a possibility on a lot of legislation, because Trump has no ideology."Whether Trump would embrace any of those proposals remains uncertain. Lowering the Medicare eligibility age would carry substantial federal costs, and the President has offered no specific commitments to expanding Medicare or reversing Medicaid reductions. But his suggestion that an agreement with Democrats might be easier than advancing legislation through budget reconciliation, a procedure that allows certain measures to bypass the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold, raised the possibility of a bipartisan alternative.“Can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want,” Trump said. “We could end up with great health care in our country.”Immigration presents a more complicated opening, particularly given Trump's decision after the election to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, to White House chief of staff. Jeffries denounced Miller as a “dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist,” underscoring the gulf between the Democratic leader and the administration.Yet Trump has said that his administration's aggressive enforcement policies may have contributed to Republicans' devastating election losses. In a recent interview with 60 Minutes, Trump conceded that deporting immigrants who had lived and worked in the United States for years may have alienated voters who otherwise supported his border security agenda. “I think it might be too tough,” Trump said of his deportation policies. “That hurt me.”He has suggested that a deal with Democrats could protect certain longtime residents who had committed no crimes beyond entering the country illegally, while preserving his administration's ability to deport people convicted of serious offenses.This week, Jeffries said the new House majority would move early next year to advance the American Dream and Promise Act, legislation that would provide a path to permanent legal residency for immigrants brought to the United States as children and certain people protected from deportation under Temporary Protected Status. Trump's friendlier tone toward Jeffries on Friday stood in sharp contrast to his history with the Democrat, whose relationship with the President has been marked by increasingly personal attacks. During a government funding dispute last year, Trump circulated an AI-generated video depicting Jeffries wearing a sombrero, which the Democratic leader denounced as racist and bigoted. Their exchanges grew even more caustic after Trump posted a video depicting former President Barack Obama and former first lady Michelle Obama as apes, prompting Jeffries to call the president an “unhinged bottom feeder.”Schumer, by contrast, has a longer personal history with Trump, dating to their years in New York politics. On Friday, Trump recalled giving Schumer what he described as his first political contribution, a $500 donation during an early campaign. “I always had a good relationship until I ran for office,” Trump said. “I was one of his backers.”“I got richer and richer and richer, and he got more successful politically,” he added. “Who knew this was going to happen?” Schumer is currently locked in a battle with Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen for the Majority Leader role, which will be determined on Dec. 1. Jeffries, facing no challenger, was elected the Speaker-designate by House Democrats this week.

items.standfirst: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude. It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

items.title: Anthropic Researcher Claims to Solve Riemann Problem With Claude
items.standfirst: On the heels of Anthropic PBC’s record-breaking initial public offering, a researcher at the company said he believes he used its artificial intelligence software to solve a famous number theory problem that has plagued mathematicians for more than 150 years.
